analysis.one_liner: Adds Medicare coverage for routine colon cancer screening tests, with set payment rates and frequency limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on November 2, 1995 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, Medicare did not pay for screening tests to catch colon cancer early. This bill would have made Medicare cover annual fecal-occult blood tests, periodic exams like flexible sigmoidoscopy or barium enema every five years for people 50 and over, and colonoscopy every two years for people at high risk. It also set specific payment caps so the new benefit would not drive up costs, and barred doctors who don't take Medicare assignment from charging patients extra beyond the standard limit.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those 50 and older or with a family history of colon cancer, would gain coverage for screening tests designed to catch colorectal cancer early, when it is most treatable. The bill sets a $5 payment limit for the annual stool blood test starting in 1996 and gives the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to adjust rates and frequencies over time.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would pay for annual screening fecal-occult blood tests, with a payment limit of no more than $5 in 1996, adjusted in later years.
People 50 and older at average risk could get a periodic screening procedure (flexible sigmoidoscopy, barium enema, or others the Secretary approves) once every five years.
People at high risk, based on family history, prior polyps or cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or genetic markers, could get screening colonoscopy or other procedures every two years.
Doctors who do not participate in Medicare could not charge patients more than the standard limiting charge for these screening services, and violators face sanctions.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare, and ultimately taxpayers and Part B enrollees through premiums, would bear the cost of a new screening benefit. Clinical laboratories would be paid no more than $5 for each screening stool blood test in 1996, a cap that could be reduced further after 1998 if the Secretary judged it more than needed to keep tests available. Nonparticipating physicians would give up the ability to bill patients above the limiting charge for these services.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new open-ended Medicare entitlement during a period when Congress was focused on restraining federal health spending, and the true cost depends on how many beneficiaries get screened.

The $5 payment cap on stool blood tests was set by statute rather than by cost data, and could be cut further after 1998, raising the risk that labs would not offer the test at that rate or would cut corners on quality.

Coverage is narrower than modern screening practice: people under 50 get nothing, and average-risk beneficiaries would not have access to screening colonoscopy, which was reserved for the high-risk category.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a real, evidence-backed one: catching colorectal cancer early saves lives, and Medicare covered none of these screening tests at the time. The costs are real but modest by entitlement standards, and the bill builds in cost controls (payment caps, frequency limits, and Secretarial review) that go further than most benefit expansions. The main design weakness is the rigid $5 lab payment cap and the exclusion of colonoscopy for average-risk patients, both of which reflect 1995-era screening practice. On balance, the benefits to seniors clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor action ever followed before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Breaux introduced the Colorectal Cancer Screening Act of 1995 in the Senate on November 2, 1995, joined by original cosponsors including Conrad, Dorgan, Kerrey, Daschle, and Hollings.
The bill had 11 cosponsors, 10 Democrats and 1 Republican.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where any Medicare legislation must start; that was the last action of any kind.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries lost a chance at covered colon cancer screening. The federal budget was spared the cost of a new benefit, and labs and physicians avoided operating under the bill's fixed payment caps. Congress as a whole avoided taking a position on expanding Medicare during a budget-cutting era.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (10 of 11 cosponsors) but included one Republican, and the record shows no floor vote or recorded opposition; the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would have created a new paid volume of Medicare screening tests, but at a statutory cap of $5 per stool blood test in 1996, with authority to cut the cap further after 1998. Labs gain a mandate-like revenue stream only if the fixed rate covers their cost.

Sigmoidoscopies, barium enemas, and high-risk colonoscopies would become billable Medicare services, expanding the pool of paying patients. In exchange, providers accept fee-schedule rates and a ban on balance-billing patients above the limiting charge for these services.
